title: Bell and Hymn
premise: Mirabel Okafor returns to the family house to bury her twin sister Miriam, only to discover the funeral is for a body that isn't hers — and that the house's founders bound something in its mirrors that feeds on grief and trades survival for memory. As every reflection lags one second behind reality, Mirabel realizes the lag is widening into a second world where Miriam may still exist. To save what remains of her sister without surrendering her own name to the house, she must complete the founders' unfinished sealing ritual before the last living resident — her dying grandmother — signs the deed that would make the house's hunger permanent. She finishes it at terrible cost: Miriam passes through once, briefly, to say goodbye, and Mirabel burns the mirrors, keeping only a shard as proof that documentation, like love, can outlast what it records.
about_author: Felix Vasquez is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six years cataloguing estate sales in coastal New England, where he developed an unhealthy respect for old houses and their paperwork. He writes horror about families who keep records of things better left unrecorded.

chapters.title: The Wrong Body
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. Arriving home for Miriam's funeral, she views the body and knows instantly it isn't her twin — same face, wrong scar, wrong hands. The family insists she's grieving badly; only her grandmother, half-lucid, whispers that 'the house takes the one who stays.' Emotional beat: disorientation curdling into dread as Mirabel begins photographing everything, her documentation habit becoming both coping mechanism and investigation.

chapters.title: One Second Late
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. The mirrors begin reflecting rooms a beat behind reality, and in the lagged images Mirabel glimpses Miriam moving through the house. Digging into the founders' papers in the attic, she finds an incomplete ritual — a binding left half-finished when the last founder died mid-signature. Emotional beat: obsessive hope; the found family of scattered cousins and the grandmother's caretaker rally around her even as the house starts punishing them for looking.

chapters.title: What the House Keeps
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV, with one interlude from inside the mirror-world. The house escalates: reflections act independently, the caretaker vanishes, and Mirabel learns the price of survival — each resident who 'made it through' traded their name and memories to the glass. Her grandmother reveals she signed decades ago and has been paying ever since. Climax builds as the deed arrives by courier, final signature pending. Emotional beat: terror braided with fierce protectiveness.

chapters.title: Sign Nothing
chapters.summary: Mirabel's POV. At the signing, Mirabel completes the founders' ritual using her documented evidence — photographs, recordings, names spoken aloud — as the binding words. The mirrors shatter; Miriam steps through for ninety seconds to say goodbye before dissolving. Mirabel keeps one shard, refuses the inheritance, and leaves with her found family. Final image: back in the city, the shard fogs, and for one second, reflects a room she isn't in. Emotional beat: grief transmuted into resolve, with a lingering, honest scar.
